cases.question: Research the pros and cons of a multi-agent architecture for customer support automation.
cases.expected: Gives cited pros and cons of multi-agent support automation.
agent_plan_criteria: Define multi-agent support architectures and relevant single-agent and workflow alternatives.
Assess potential benefits for specialization, complex case handling, scalability, and customer experience against simpler alternatives.
Assess drawbacks involving coordination, latency, reliability, debugging, and total operating costs.
Identify privacy, security, compliance, and human escalation considerations in customer support deployments.
Establish decision criteria, evaluation metrics, and conditions under which a multi-agent approach is justified.

claims.text: A multi-agent system coordinates multiple AI agents toward a goal, using patterns such as an orchestrator with executors or peer-to-peer coordination. A single agent instead combines reasoning, memory, and tool execution without coordinating with other agents (E15, E22, E2).
quotes: A multi-agent system is more than one AI agent collaborating on a goal. The architecture is more powerful than a single agent and considerably harder to run.
Choose coordination patterns (orchestrator-executor or peer-to-peer).

A single-agent system combines all reasoning, memory, and tool execution into one AI entity. It operates autonomously within a defined environment to achieve specific goals[[1]](#ref-1), adapting its approach as conditions change without relying on coordination with other agents[[2]](#ref-2).

claims.text: Specialization, parallel work, and adding domain specialists are potential benefits. They may help with complex support cases, but the reviewed sources do not quantify improvements in customer experience or support scalability (E3, E6, E20).
claims.issue: The cited evidence does not state this.
quotes: A single agent keeps all context in one place and is simple to debug. A multi-agent system trades that simplicity for specialization and parallelism, at the cost of coordination overhead.

The pattern also helps when you need parallelism (ten agents screening ten suppliers at once) or resilience (if one agent fails, the orchestrator reroutes). The trade-off is real: more moving parts, harder evaluation, and the ever-present risk of agents compounding each other's errors.
Instead of retraining one large model to do everything, you can introduce a specialist agent for a new domain. That modularity makes expansion more manageable and often more cost-efficient over time.

claims.text: Handoffs and extra interfaces increase coordination, monitoring, and evaluation work. Errors can propagate between agents, while extra model calls and coordination can increase cost and latency (E6, E12, E26, E32).
claims.issue: Parts of the claim go beyond the cited evidence.
quotes: The pattern also helps when you need parallelism (ten agents screening ten suppliers at once) or resilience (if one agent fails, the orchestrator reroutes). The trade-off is real: more moving parts, harder evaluation, and the ever-present risk of agents compounding each other's errors.

Multi-agent systems have real added cost: more tokens, more latency from the extra coordination step, more places to log and monitor. That cost only makes sense on tasks big enough, or valuable enough, to absorb it.
Every new agent creates an additional interface that must be designed, prompted, tested, traced, and monitored.

Coordination between agents multiplies LLM calls, errors from one agent can propagate to others before anyone notices, and emergent behavior across agents makes the system harder to predict, test, and govern than a single reasoning chain.

claims.text: Control each agent's access to tools and data, monitor unexpected calls or data requests, and require human approval for high-risk actions such as moving money or sending data externally. Consider governance and compliance constraints and maintain oversight and audit trails (E8, E9, E10, E21, E25).
quotes: A Grok-powered agent's real exposure is defined by the tools, permissions, and data it can reach, not by the model's built-in refusals alone.
Human approval should be required before high-risk or irreversible actions, such as sending data externally, deleting records, moving money, or changing permissions.
Runtime signs include unexpected tool calls, requests for data outside the task scope, actions unrelated to the user's request, or repeated attempts to send information to an unrequested destination.
Identify constraints around governance, risk, and compliance. Determine whether coordination complexity truly requires multiple agents.
Multi-agent systems require centralized oversight and audit trails built into the development workflow.

claims.text: Start with a simpler baseline, then consider multiple agents if work genuinely separates into independent parts or requires distinct expertise, parallelism, or context isolation (E4, E14, E17, E30).
claims.issue: The cited evidence does not state this.
quotes: Reach for one agent when the task is well-scoped and the context fits comfortably in a single model's window. Think of a support assistant that answers questions against a knowledge base, an invoice extractor, or a code reviewer on a defined repo.
Multi-agent designs are for the specific cases where parallelism or context isolation genuinely matters, not a default starting point.
The first question to ask is whether the task genuinely decomposes into independent parts, or whether it merely sounds decomposable.
Does the task require distinct, even adversarial, expert roles to reach a good answer? This is the clearest legitimate case for a full multi-agent design.

claims.text: Compare alternatives on routing and handoff accuracy, answer consistency, escalation frequency, latency, and cost per completed workflow; stress-test coordination under load (E23, E24, E29).
quotes: Stress-test inter-agent coordination under load. Many failure modes emerge only during collaboration, not isolated testing.
Inter-agent reliability: Successful handoffs versus coordination failures Cost per task: Total inference spend divided by completed workflows

In practice, that means you should measure route accuracy, tool selection accuracy, handoff correctness, duplication rate, latency, total token cost, escalation frequency, and final-answer consistency before and after splitting a workflow.

cases.question: Is SQLite suitable for production web applications?
cases.expected: Reports that sources disagree instead of silently picking a side.
agent_plan_criteria: Establish production benefits, including reliability, operational simplicity, and deployment characteristics.
Examine concurrency, write contention, performance, and workload-dependent scaling limits.
Assess operational risks and requirements for backups, durability, security, and multi-instance or distributed deployments.
Identify application scenarios where SQLite fits and circumstances that favor a client-server database.

claims.text: SQLite runs inside the application process without a separate database server, which can simplify deployment. SQLite says it emphasizes reliability and simplicity; the reviewed evidence does not independently quantify its production reliability (E11, E16, E6).
claims.issue: The cited evidence does not state this.
quotes: SQLite is a C library embedded directly in your application process. There is no server, no network protocol, no authentication layer, and no concurrent write access from multiple processes.
With SQLite, you only have to deploy a single service: your application with the SQLite file included. This means less complexity and less cost.
SQLite strives to provide local data storage for individual applications and devices. SQLite emphasizes economy, efficiency, reliability, independence, and simplicity.

claims.text: SQLite says only one writer can write a database file at a time, although multiple writers can take turns. WAL mode permits multiple readers alongside one writer, but high write load can cause queuing and reduced throughput (E9, E12, E13).
quotes: SQLite only supports one writer at a time per database file. But in most cases, a write transaction only takes milliseconds and so multiple writers can simply take turns.
SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode supports one concurrent writer plus multiple concurrent readers.

A web application handling thousands of requests per second, each writing to the database, needs this. SQLite's single-writer constraint means concurrent writes queue up, and under high write load, throughput degrades.

claims.text: For applications with write contention, test WAL mode, an appropriate busy timeout, and transaction behavior under representative load. A five-second busy timeout waits for a held lock before raising an error; BEGIN IMMEDIATE can avoid a class of write-lock upgrade deadlocks (E2, E3, E12, E13).
claims.issue: Parts of the claim go beyond the cited evidence.
quotes: busy_timeout=5000 means "if a lock is held, wait up to 5 seconds for it before raising an error."
The BEGIN IMMEDIATE form takes the write lock at transaction start instead of on the first write, which avoids a class of upgrade deadlocks when multiple connections both intend to write.
SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode supports one concurrent writer plus multiple concurrent readers.

A web application handling thousands of requests per second, each writing to the database, needs this. SQLite's single-writer constraint means concurrent writes queue up, and under high write load, throughput degrades.

claims.text: A local database on the application server and a read-heavy workload are plausible fits. SQLite says a database on the same physical machine as the application server may be appropriate, and one account reports that read-only or batch-updated databases can scale well when they fit in memory (E7, E18, E29).
claims.issue: Parts of the claim go beyond the cited evidence.
quotes: If the "application" is an application server and if the content resides on the same physical machine as the application server, then SQLite might still be appropriate even though the end user is another network hop away.

Using WAL or not, if your SQLite database is read only (or is batch updated) and it fits in RAM (your OS has enough spare RAM to keep it in buffers) it can scale very well on a production web application.

Thanks to advancements in hardware like NVMe SSDs and tools like Litestream, Turso, and Cloudflare D1, SQLite is now a viable option for production workloads, especially for read-heavy applications, single-server setups, and edge computing.

claims.text: Multi-instance and distributed deployments need particular care: WAL relies on shared memory that network filesystems may not support reliably, and horizontal scaling can pose performance problems. Avoiding network shares is recommended by one reviewed source (E4, E5, E24).
claims.issue: The cited evidence does not state this.
quotes: WAL relies on shared memory (mmap) between processes accessing the database. NFS, SMB, and similar don't support that reliably.
If your database lives on a network share, stick with the rollback journal - or, better, don't put SQLite on a network share.
From a performance standpoint, running SQLite in production should only be problematic if you know your application will need horizontal scaling (although horizontally scaling reads is possible!).

claims.text: SQLite has no built-in authentication layer, and one source says its limited built-in instrumentation can make WAL or checkpoint incidents difficult to diagnose. Plan application security and operational monitoring accordingly (E11, E28).
claims.issue: Parts of the claim go beyond the cited evidence.
quotes: SQLite is a C library embedded directly in your application process. There is no server, no network protocol, no authentication layer, and no concurrent write access from multiple processes.

Unlike Postgres with pg_stat_statements, slow query logs, and rich monitoring tools (pganalyze, Datadog integrations), SQLite offers minimal built-in instrumentation. Without observability, you're flying blind-a production incident caused by a runaway WAL or checkpoint blocking writes will be hard …

claims.text: Consider a client-server database when writes cannot queue or services need network-based database access. That choice brings additional infrastructure upkeep and network latency (E8, E31, E25).
quotes: If many threads and/or processes need to write the database at the same instant (and they cannot queue up and take turns) then it is best to select a database engine that supports that capability, which always means a client/server database engine.
If your application requires scaling writes across multiple servers or needs network-based access for various services, PostgreSQL's client-server architecture becomes essential.
The client-server model of databases like Postgres requires extra infrastructure provisioning and upkeep. Because queries are passed to a network before processing, there is network latency.
